newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mahathir says Malaysia-Singapore row not "major".
newsitem.headline: Mahathir says Malaysia-Singapore row not "major".

text.p: Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad cautiously broke his silence about the new flare-up between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore on Thursday, saying the issue was not a major problem and would be overcome with time.

Gingerly stepping round cabinet decisions taken in Kuala Lumpur while he was on a visit to Tokyo, Mahathir made clear, however, that derogatory remarks by Singapore's elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew still rankled Malaysians.

Media reports on Wednesday had said Malaysia was freezing ties with Singapore, including the awarding of new contracts to Singapore firms, because of remarks by other Singaporean leaders since Lee apologised last week for describing Malaysia's Johor state as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".

But in Kuala Lumpur on Thursday, Malaysian Minister of Works S. Samy Vellu put a less dramatic spin on the issue, saying the government had not frozen ties with Singapore, just suspended a culture and sports agreement.
Also, acting foreign minister Abang Abu Bakar Abang Mustapha said that, "no decision has been made to freeze ties with Singapore as reported by the local newspapers."

Although the Malaysian cabinet discussed ties between the countries, "I would like to stress that whatever has been reported by the mass media as their main subject in the leading local newspapers today (Thursday) are not accurate," he said.
Questioned at a Tokyo news conference about the first reports of a serious rupture, Mahathir kept his options open.
"I would like to know more about this before I explain the reason why. They (cabinet ministers) must have had some reason for making this decision," he said.
"But I don't think this is a major problem," Mahathir said on the second day of a four-day visit to Japan.
"Naturally between neighbours there will be differences off and on, but over time this feeling can be overcome," he added.
But Mahathir did not flinch from saying Lee's remarks were still an issue in ties between Singapore and Malaysia.
"Relationships with Singapore will resume as soon as people get over the feeling of hurt and bitterness caused by uncalled for remarks against Malaysia," he said.
The original row erupted after Lee, in a court affidavit leaked to the Malaysian press, described the southern state of Johor as a "notorious" place.

Lee apologised and instructed his lawyer to ask the court to delete the remarks from a deposition in a libel suit against a Singaporean opposition politician who fled to Johor after saying he had received death threats in Singapore.
Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong played for time in the confusion.
"I think I want to take some time to understand Malaysia's reaction before I comment," he told reporters on Thursday after talks with visiting Australian Prime Minister John Howard.
"I want to absorb the implications of all this before I give my comments," Goh said.
During a visit to Laos earlier this week, Goh had said it was time for Singapore and Malaysia "to move on" after Malaysia accepted Lee's "unreserved apology".
"There is a Malay saying that water cannot be separated, even with a knife. This is the nature of our relations with Malaysia," he was quoted as saying in Laos by Singapore media.
